newsitem.title: PERU: One hostage out in Peru, 105 stay for Christmas.
newsitem.headline: One hostage out in Peru, 105 stay for Christmas.

text.p: One hostage was released by Marxist rebels on Tuesday evening after a week at the besieged Japanese embassy residence in Peru, but the other 105 prisoners seemed set to spend Christmas there.
His head bowed, Uruguayan ambassador Tabare Bocalandro walked to freedom from the building accompanied by chief Red Cross mediator Michel Minnig and sped away in a police car.
Ambassador Bocalandro's release came the same day as Uruguay set free two prisoners from the same guerrilla group as the hostage-takers, the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA).
There was no official confirmation the two events were linked but government sources in Montevideo hinted a deal had been cut.
Freedom for more than 400 Tupac Amaru prisoners in Peruvian jails has been the main demand of the rebels since they stormed the residence last Tuesday, initally taking around 500 prisoners.

Minnig told reporters 105 captives of different nationalities remained inside, a lower figure than previously given. Red Cross officials attributed the change to earlier confusion but said they were confident of the new figure.
Peruvians prayed for a Christmas miracle to set the remaining hostages free and family members sent messages over the airwaves to their loved ones.

"Brother, I'm sending you a huge hug...God bless you, have faith like us, have hope that everything will end well," said Leonor Siura, the sister of captive Peruvian congressman Gilberto Siura, in a radio message.

"We can't go and celebrate Christmas knowing they are all in there," Tania Verdeguer, a friend of one of the hostages, told Reuters as she prayed for the captives near press lines, candles burning on the sidewalk before her.

Hostages got a crumb of Christmas comfort when the Red Cross piped water from a tanker into the residence, allowing hostages and rebels to flush toilets for the first time in days. Flashlights were also to be allowed in for the first time since power was cut last Saturday. Water and telephone lines were cut off at the same time.
Helpers unloaded an oriental food dinner and orange juice for the hostages and delivered letters from relatives.
A captive Jesuit priest, Juan Julio Wicht, prepared to celebrate Christmas mass inside as he had done last Sunday.
Wicht refused an offer to leave with the last big group of hostages set free on Sunday because he believed his duty was to stay behind and minister to the captives.

Most have now been released, including all the Europeans and Americans. However, six ambassadors, 30 Japanese and dozens of top Peruvians including President Alberto Fujimori's brother, Pedro, two ministers and the anti-terrorism police chief remain hostages.

Fujimori, whose father emigrated to Peru from Japan, has flatly rejected all the rebel demands; but he assured Pope John Paul II in a message on Tuesday that he wanted a peaceful solution to the crisis.
Prospects for more releases looked grim, with no sign of negotiations between the government and the roughly 20 muscular young rebels.
No communication has come from the hostage-takers since Sunday night, when they released most of their captives in what they termed a humanitarian gesture at Christmas time.

Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, whose government has most at stake in the affair after Peru because of the large number of Japanese hostages, predicted on Tuesday that the hostage crisis would be a long, drawn-out affair.
Lima would try to wear the guerrillas down rather than flush them out by force, he said.

Fujimori told the rebels to surrender and release all their hostages in a stern message on Saturday but since then the government has given no official information to the hordes of waiting world media.
Diplomats speculated that the government might be secretly negotiating a safe passage to Cuba for the rebels in exchange for the release of all hostages. There was no official confirmation.
